description: The Argument (Part IV conclusion): raw trace data → explicit argument structure. Meta-level wiring diagram for the Strategy Patterns chapter, showing how git commit traces become an argumentative structure (AIF), and how the sidebar live case study validates the metacognitive interrupt claim.

nodes.body_text: Raw data: git hashes and commit traces from the ten-problem sprint.
Evidence ledgers: pattern-tagged commit support. Each of five design patterns has an evidence ledger citing 3–5 pivotal commits with roles and primary artifacts.

Post-hoc reconstruction: pattern extraction from chronology. Five design patterns (Outcome Typing, Layer-Switching, Creative Reduction, Structural Decomposition, Layer Switch Under Coaching) extracted from the sprint's commit history.

Conclusion claim: textual argument recovers strategy-level causality. The evidence ledgers and patterns constitute an argument that the sprint's proof strategies are causally recoverable from the commit trace.

Canonical episode (Problem 6): persistence → obstruction → layer switch → progress. The full P6 arc from dispatch-driven GPL-H attack through coaching intervention to elementary proof via Turán + Foster + pigeonhole.

Cross-problem learning: strategy-level analogy. Transfer operates at the level of proof strategy, not mathematical content — P7's layer-switching strategy transfers to P6 even though the mathematics is entirely different.

AIF node types: claim / conflict / preference / inference. The Argument Interchange Framework provides typed nodes for representing argument structure. P6's five-node worked example: n1 (claim: BSS adapts), n2 (conflict: structural obstruction), n3 (preference: switch layer), n4 (claim: elementary proof), n5 (inference: n4 resolves what n2 blocked).

Typed edges: attacks / supports / preference-over. AIF edges capture argumentative relations: n2 →[attacks] n1, n3 →[preference] n4 over n1, n5 →[supports] n4. Three edges suffice for the P6 layer-switch argument.
S-expression form: math content + argument structure together. (aif:graph (node n1 :type claim :content "BSS adapts") (edge n2 n1 :type attacks) ...) — no separate annotation layer needed.
Arxana (futon5): typed-edge graph substrate. Provides persistent storage for the AIF graph with typed nodes and edges. The S-expression form maps directly to Arxana's native representation.

Peripheral model (futon3c): explore → reflect → edit → reflect → test. Constrained execution environments where reflect hops produce argumentative annotation because that is the only permitted action. The constraint makes reflection generative rather than reflexive.

(layer, status) monitor: detect stationarity. Track (layer, status) pairs across commits; flag stationarity after k cycles to trigger reframing prompt automatically. P6's failed phase exhibits the TryHarder signature: six dispatch-and-fail cycles over eight hours, all in the sparsification layer.

Learning from success: visible closures; coach not dispatch. Make success histories visible to stuck agents — rumination is not learning, analogy is. Coach with reframing questions ('What kind of problem is this?'), don't dispatch another attack vector.

Stuck phase: hours in one layer, no closure. After P6's elementary proof for K_n, agents spent several hours exploring amplification bounds (trajectory coupling, Neumann expansion, spectral spread) within the barrier-greedy layer. (layer, status) = (barrier-greedy amplification, open) was stationary.

Intervention: second-agent MathOverflow scan. During writing of Part IV — while editing the very paragraphs about metacognitive interrupts — a second agent scanned 152,893 MO questions across six independent strategy tracks (A–F), each with keyword bundles and contextual anchoring.

Result: split replaces single bound target. E-regime (graph-adaptive transfer, deg_{R,max} ≤ 2) + F-regime (gain-loss balance, deg_{R,max} ≥ 3) replaces the single universal amplification bound. Track E dominated with 60 anchored-strong hits vs 8 for next-best.

Demonstration: reflect hop changes policy faster. The MO scan was structurally a reflect hop — constrained task (read external literature, do not edit proof) that returned with annotation (alternative approaches, ranked by precedent). It produced a genuine layer switch in under 30 minutes after five hours of local play.

Cycle 7: BMI falsified in general graphs. The barrier-monotonicity inequality d̄_t < 1 was disproved for general graphs via explicit construction. The Turán + Foster + pigeonhole construction still works; the target shifts from BMI to vertex-level feasibility (No-Skip / GPL-V).

Status code: OPEN / STUCK / FALSIFIED. The (layer, status) monitor should track three states. FALSIFIED is distinct from STUCK — it means the layer is proven impossible, not just difficult. The BMI falsification is the concrete instance.

Control rule: FALSIFIED ⇒ abandon layer. A FALSIFIED status should trigger layer abandonment, not just reframing. This is the strongest form of the metacognitive interrupt — the layer itself is dead, not merely stuck.

Metacognitive interrupt: trigger policy switch on stationarity/falsification. Four independent paths converge: the sidebar demonstration, the postscript control rule, the learning-from-success principle, and the (layer, status) monitor. The git log provides the detection signal — repeated commits within the same layer with no status change is the TryHarder signature.

THE ARGUMENT: raw trace data → explicit argument structure. The ten-problem sprint demonstrates that strategy-level causality is recoverable from commit traces, and that the argumentative structure can be formalized via AIF node/edge typing and S-expression representation.

Target system: live AIF graph; patterns become graph queries. With Arxana (typed-edge storage) + peripheral model (real-time capture via reflect hops) + S-expression form (unified representation), the sprint's argumentative structure would be captured as it unfolds — the distance is a tooling gap, not a conceptual one.
